#2790. How a third-quarter run amplified the Lakers’ resiliency

LOS ANGELES — Luka Dončić stepped up to the free throw line in the third quarter.

The Lakers' NBA Cup court plastered in gold. The crowd an ocean of the same color. Dončić was engulfed, but instead of the sound of waves flooding the senses, it was the MVP chants, each growing louder than the next.

Dončić made his first, marking his 40th point of the game and 20th in the quarter, capping off a 34-15 run in the frame that brought Los Angeles back from a 16-point deficit and gave them an 87-75 lead over the Portland Trail Blazers.

It was a run that put the Lakers in front heading into the final frame and helped them exact revenge on a Blazers side that handed them one of their two losses as they won 124-118 on Friday.

"Anytime you start a half down, you want to get to momentum early," head coach JJ Redick said of the third quarter. "We were playing from behind the first half, so I thought it was really important to get off to a good start, and we did that. … for the most part, it felt like we had control of the rest of the game, and a lot of that had to do with how we defended in the third quarter."

It's impossible to gloss over Dončić in this game, who finished with 53 points on 17-of-33 shooting from the field, passing Kareem Abdul-Jabbar for the 10th-most 50-point games in NBA history. The Lakers made their run and took control in the third quarter, but the momentum shifted when Dončić drained a shot from the opposite 3-point line as time expired in the first half.

"[That shot] changes the whole energy," Dončić said postgame. "In the team and in the gym. That was an important shot to make. So that's why I decided to make it."

At the time, the Lakers had made just three of their 23 3-point attempts and were enduring what looked like the game where the offense inevitably regressed to the mean. Instead, including Dončić's heave, Los Angeles made eight of their last 14 deep shots en route to a much-needed win.

Redick has preached patience and steady incline as a team all year, but a win like this for sole position at the top of the Western Conference — and on NBA Cup night no less — was a clear measure of their resilience.

And yet, Redick thinks they're still building.

"I think we're already a really together group," he added Friday. "You don't become a resilient team in 10 games, five games, 20 games. It takes a full season to build that resiliency. … But, the fact that this is a very together group and we've already shown a level of resiliency, it's exciting, it's promising and I want to continue building on that."

Much of this lands on Dončić's shoulders. He's having a historical season, one of the best we've ever seen, but he's a product of the team around him. It's a roster he had his hands all over, collectively crafted around his needs at every corner, a point driven by Portland head coach Micah Nori before they clashed on Friday.

Nori says it's Dončić's MVP to lose, "hands down," but because of everything around him. The shooting, the defending, Walker Kessler's rolling. It's all working in unison.

The Lakers have 72 games to go. It's not always going to be like this. But again, a night like Friday works wonders for the marathon Redick is trying to run.

"We all want good results," he said. "This is going to be a long process and it's going to take time for us to become a great basketball team. I like that our guys have responded to some adversity. Tonight was a great example, where we get down pretty big early and we just stick with it."

You can follow Connor on Twitter at @cmorenoNBA.

#2789. 2026-27 NHL season predictions: Expert picks for Stanley Cup playoffs, champion and major awards this season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Following a brief offseason and an expedited preseason, the 2026-27 NHL season has arrived. Before the puck drops on opening night, we have some predictions to make.

If this season feel like it's staring earlier than usual, that's because it is. The NHL is adopting an 84-game regular season, which just means more hockey for the rest of us. That also means a long and arduous journey to the Stanley Cup is ever so slightly more difficult.

So, what will that journey look like? The Carolina Hurricanes are looking to defend their title as Cup champions, but they'll have to contend with a deep Eastern Conference and some real juggernauts in the Western Conference. With that in mind, we logged our expert predictions for the playoff field in each conference -- and there were a few surprises -- before making our Stanley Cup Final selections.

We also called our shot on the winners of each major individual award. Connor McDavid is looking for his fourth Hart Trophy, but he's got some competition from an up-and-coming superstar in his own division. Races for the Norris Trophy and Vezina Trophy should be pretty wide open, and unexpected candidates always emerge throughout the season.

It should be a fun season in the NHL, so follow along with all our coverage at CBS Sports. Let's get things kicked off with the season preview and predictions, which will of course be 100% accurate.

Baumgartner: I don't see many new faces entering the conversation when it comes to the Eastern Conference playoff race. A healthy Florida Panthers side will slot themselves right back towards the top of the Atlantic, and a revamped Washington Capitals side should be able to make some noise in the Metropolitan. Besides that, I have six 2026 playoff teams returning to the dance in 2027.

Nivison: As much as I hate to go with chalk in preseason predictions -- because it rarely happens that way -- there's no denying the top dogs in the West. The Avalanche and Stars are the class of the Central Division, and the Golden Knights should pound a pitiful Pacific Division into a pulp. Things get more interesting behind those clear Cup contenders, and I'm projecting another significant leap forward from the Mammoth. I also think Macklin Celebrini will be successful in dragging the Sharks to the playoffs in his third NHL season.

Nivison -- Columbus Blue Jackets: The Blue Jackets have been agonizingly close to the playoffs in each of the last two seasons, and I think they get over the hump in 2026-27. There are still questions in Columbus. Can Adam Fantilli be a franchise player at center? Is the forward group as a whole good enough to keep pace in a competitive Eastern Conference? Still, I am sure the Blue Jackets have a really strong blue line, led by Norris Trophy winner Zach Werenski, and goaltender Jet Greaves is on track to become a Vezina Trophy candidate. Internal improvements from the young core will then get Columbus above the cut line.

Baumgartner -- San Jose Sharks: The Sharks narrowly missed out on the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, finishing just four points short of the second wild card. San Jose added a good group of veterans over the summer, but the most important offseason move was selecting Ivar Stenberg with the No. 2 pick in the Draft. Stenberg joins the youth movement in San Jose, which is spearheaded by new captain Macklin Celebrini, who broke the Sharks single-season points record with 115 last season. The Sharks are a better team than they were last year, and with Celebrini entering his third season as a legit Hart Trophy contender, this team won't be fun to play against.

Nivison: Yes, the Mammoth have a brutal path coming out of the Central Divison, but just close your eyes and imagine this scenario with me. Logan Cooley becomes a superstar center. Dylan Guenther hits 50 goals. Dmitry Simashev asserts himself as a budding top-four defenseman. Anders Lee and Vincent Trocheck provide necessary veteran depth. Now open your eyes. Utah is your Western Conference champion.

Unfortunately for the Mammoth, they will run into a refreshed Panthers team that now has double-barreled Tkachuks. Last season, we found out that all it takes to stop Florida is to hope all of its key players miss significant time with injury. The long offseason was probably a blessing in disguise as it allowed the Panthers to get healthy, and that's bad news for everyone else. The structure in front of the crease will limit some of the volatility we saw from Jacob Markstrom in New Jersey, and Florida wins its third Stanley Cup in four years.

Baumgartner: Before last season, the Carolina Hurricanes' kryptonite was the Eastern Conference Final. The Hurricanes were able to overcome their demons and win the East before ultimately taking home the franchise's first Stanley Cup since 2006. In the West, the Dallas Stars have been running into the same problem. After three straight seasons ending in the Western Conference Final, the Stars regressed last postseason, flaming out in the first-round to the Minnesota Wild. The Central Division will once again be a gauntlet, but I'm ready for Dallas to take the next step and reach the Stanley Cup Final.

While Dallas has continued to fall short in recent years, the Panthers have done the opposite. The Panthers made three consecutive Stanley Cup Final appearances, winning back-to-back Cups in 2023-24 and 2024-25. Last season, Florida's three-peat attempt came to a halt on day one of training after captain Aleksander Barkov went down with a non-contact injury, tearing both the ACL and MCL in his right knee. An offseason of healing for Barkov, and the rest of the banged up Panthers, has the team refreshed entering September for the first time in years. With nearly the entire 2025 Stanley Cup winning core still on the team and Brady Tkachuk added to the fold, Florida looks ready to win its third Stanley Cup in four seasons.

Nivison: Celebrini should have won the Hart Trophy last season, but for some incomprehensible reason, he wasn't even a finalist. This year, Celebrini replicates that performance and gets San Jose to the postseason to take home his first MVP award at age 20. Hughes posts a career year in his first full season with the Wild, and Spencer Carberry gets his flowers for winning the Metro Division after missing the playoffs last year.

Baumgartner: McDavid's ability to take over a game was evident nearly every time he touched the ice last season. His 24 points (11 goals,13 assists) in the final 14 games of the regular season -- without Leon Draisaitl in the lineup -- was one of the many reasons I put him No. 1 on my Hart Trophy ballot. With just two years left on his current contract, desperation may start to kick in to get the job in Edmonton, which would lead to another MVP-caliber season. Barkov is healthy and the frontrunner to win his fourth Selke, and Dahlin will have another strong season to take home his first career Norris Trophy.

The New York Yankees have won 27 World Series titles, while the Boston Red Sox have nine championships to their name. But the bitter rivals are dead even when it comes to playoff matchups, and one looks to take the first step toward gaining the upper hand on Tuesday.

The teams also squared off in this round last year, with New York winning the series 2-1.

That triumph tied the clubs at three wins apiece in playoff matchups. The Yankees also defeated the Red Sox in the 1999 and 2003 AL Championship Series, while Boston was victorious in the 2004 ALCS, the 2018 AL Division Series and the AL Wild Card Game in 2021.

New York took the regular-season series in 2026, finishing with a 7-6 record after outscoring Boston 25-3 in winning the final two games. The Yankees won four of their six matchups in the Bronx.

If New York hopes to advance to the ALDS, it will have to get past Boston without three-time AL MVP Aaron Judge, who was left off the team's wild card roster. The slugger, who returned to the club on Sept. 8 after missing more than three months with a fractured rib, was placed back on the injured list just eight days later with a strained right calf.

AL Cy Young Award favorite Cam Schlittler (14-6, AL-best 1.95 ERA) will start for New York. The 25-year-old right-hander went 2-1 with a minuscule 0.74 ERA in four turns against the Red Sox this year. He will be opposed by left-hander Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.03), who hasn't lost since July 1 (5-0 in 13 outings) and gave up one run over 13 innings while going 1-0 in two starts against the Yankees in 2026.

A National League Wild Card Series also begins Tuesday night as the San Diego Padres (91-71) host the Chicago Cubs (89-73) at 10 p.m. ET at Petco Park. The Cubs dominated the season series between the clubs, winning the final five games after dropping the opener. Chicago outscored San Diego 32-10 over the final two contests.

Right-hander Michael King (12-10, 3.21) will be on the mound for the Padres. The 31-year-old posted a 2.74 ERA at home this year and allowed a total of five runs across 32 innings while going 4-0 over five starts before yielding five in four frames of a loss to the Los Angeles Dodgers in his regular-season finale. Chicago counters with southpaw Matthew Boyd (10-5, 3.91), who won his final two turns and went 1-0 in two starts against San Diego despite surrendering eight runs over nine innings.

#2783. How to Watch the Iowa Hawkeyes at Northwestern Wildcats

Your Iowa Hawkeyes are on the road to Evanston, Illinois to square off with the Northwestern Wildcats under the lights of the new Ryan Field.

Iowa and Northwestern meet tonight for the 87th time with matching 6-2 records, matching 3-2 league marks and one incredibly narrow playoff lane between them. The Hawkeyes arrive fresh off a 30-0 shutout of Wisconsin and a #19 debut in the first College Football Playoff rankings. The Wildcats return home again after a competitive loss at Oregon knocked them out of the polls. They'll be coming back to the new Ryan Field, where Northwestern has won all five games it has played this season.

This one was poised to be a proverbial shootout, by former Big Ten West standards. The Cats come into the day with the 84th ranked total defense nationally. They're 75th against the run, 94th against the pass and tied for 100th in sacks with 13 all season. After getting right against Wisconsin a week ago, this one should be an opportunity for the Hawkeye offense to build some momentum.

The real challenge comes on the other side of the ball, where new offensive coordinator Chip Kelly has things humming for the Wildcats. Northwestern is top-35 nationally in scoring offense, averaging 33.6 points per game and a top-30 in total offense at 438.1 yards per game.

But Friday afternoon, ESPN's Pete Thamel reported that Northwestern quarterback Aidan Chiles is expected to miss tonight's game with an upper body injury, with no timeline for his return. Chiles had been listed as questionable on the Wednesday and Thursday availability reports, and as of Friday night Northwestern had made no official announcement – but every beat writer on both sides is preparing for a Wildcats offense without its engine.

It's hard to overstate how big that is. Chiles has completed 68.8% of his passes for 1,898 yards with 13 touchdowns against a single interception, added 274 rushing yards and a team-best 10 scores on the ground and owns the third-best passer rating in the Big Ten. He accounted for five touchdowns in a game twice this season, picking up conference player of the week honors both times. Chip Kelly's offense hums because of him.

That leaves it to Nicco Marchiol. The left-handed West Virginia transfer lost the camp battle to Chiles in August and has thrown exactly one pass in purple, an incompletion in garbage time. The resume isn't empty – he went 6-2 as a starter for the Mountaineers and completed 62% of his career passes there. But his 2025 season ended with a foot injury after four starts and tonight would be his first start in more than a year, against a defense that just posted a shutout.

What does it mean for the game plan? Well, the quarterback run game that produced 10 of Northwestern's rushing touchdowns is now a question mark, so expect heavier doses of Caleb Komolafe and Joseph Himon II – and expect Phil Parker to pack the box and make a backup making his first start beat the fourth-ranked scoring defense in the country through the air. I'd also expect Parker to be pretty vanilla in the first half while he figures out just how to tighten the screws against Marchiol without exposing the secondary too much with Kelly looking for options. Then the pressure is likely to be dialed up in the second half.

The betting market did the math immediately. This line opened at Northwestern -2.5 and sat at -3 as late as midweek. On the news Friday afternoon it had flipped all the way to Iowa, with FanDuel at Iowa -1.5 and the total down to 43.5 off its midweek high of 45.5. The market just priced one quarterback at roughly five points.

Iowa isn't at full strength either. Center Cael Winter is out, handing Michael Myslinski his first start in the middle of the line. Zach Lutmer and Jaylen Watson are questionable in the secondary and Kirk Ferentz said this week that an unusually high number of players were held out of practice. Winning ugly on the road may require some depth tonight.

As we countdown to kickoff, here's everything you need to know about today's matchup.

#2780. Cavs forward Dean Wade expected to be back in Cleveland this season

The Cleveland Cavaliers, like a few other teams, found themselves completely preoccupied this summer with courting LeBron James. In the process, they were unwilling or unable to give Dean Wade a financial commitment.

"I kind of thought I'd probably just come back," Wade said after playing his first game in Cleveland this season. "Unfortunately, that didn't happen."

Perhaps the Cavs would have elected to move on from Wade either way. He had run his course in Cleveland, and the Cavs clearly wanted to find an upgrade at small forward. That's certainly part of the equation.

But it also seems possible that Cleveland was holding out for LeBron — and Wade leaving was a product of that waiting game.

Regardless of how it happened, Wade says he's happy with the end result.

"Philly's awesome, this team is always great, high-character people," said Wade. "It's weird going to a new place with me, like 1,000 new faces and stuff. But after a couple of weeks, it gets a lot easier. So I'm pretty happy with my decision."

Wade played seven seasons with the Cavaliers, going from an undrafted prospect in 2019 to a starter in the playoffs. This was his first time entering Rocket Arena as an enemy.

"It was weird; emotions were high, and it was pretty hard to stay focused," said Wade. "But it was good. I was happy to see everybody."

The Cavs leaned on Wade for his defense throughout the last seven seasons. But his progression from a fringe NBA player to a legitimate rotational piece is worth remembering. He's a developmental success story that helped bolster the Cavs for nearly a decade.

"Above all, you loved the person, loved the family; they're just incredible," Cavs coach Kenny Atkinson said of Wade. "Great for our culture, obviously the player, he's a heck of a player, helped us a lot even before I got here, a major player for the team — happy he landed in a good spot."

Wade is now playing a similar role in Philly, while the Cavs are hoping Peyton Watson will be everything they've needed at small forward. It's a breakup that has zero hard feelings on either end.

#2775. Swanson: Luka Doncic can lead Lakers to title if they can help get him there

Luka Doncic is hooping like he intends to run away with the MVP trophy. Making a point by scoring more points to start a season — 361 in nine games — than anyone since Wilt Chamberlain scored 472 in 1962.

Generational scoring run or the new normal? Could this historic meteor shower be the standard?

"I feel like that," Doncic said, adding he thinks he can maintain his current 40.1-points-per-game tear. "But as long as we win, I'm good."

And if he's this good when the playoffs roll around, this undeniable, brushing off elite defenders Toumani Camara and Jrue Holiday en route to 53 points in Friday's 124-118 victory over the Portland Trail Blazers, then the Lakers could totally go on a Luka Magical run and win it all.

But if Doncic is not this good, the Lakers aren't 8-2 right now, and they're not sitting in first in the Western Conference standings out of the gate … with 72 more games to go.

There's ability, there's inevitability, bankability.

Read more: Luka Doncic scores 53 as Lakers avenge loss to Trail Blazers

The Lakers are going to need to employ some serious conservation measures to get this version of Doncic — whose seven consecutive 35-points or better games put him on par with Elgin Baylor and Kobe Bryant as the only Lakers to stack so many in regular-season history — to the starting line that matters.

They need to write to Santa Claus and ask for a serviceable backup center. They need Austin Reaves to really rock and roll with the units that don't include Doncic — who has the highest plus-minus and the highest on/off rating in the NBA — and to keep his turnover tallies low. They need to not just beat but blow out bad teams, to give Doncic a fourth quarter off sometimes.

And they need coach JJ Redick — who boasted in September that the Lakers' "naturally deeper roster" would result in a longer rotation — to trust the process.

Even if the amount of "my bad" from his backups costs the Lakers some regular-season wins, it will, on occasion, make more sense to punt than to go for it. Like when you're readying a less-experienced, less-familiar team for future battles. And wanting to reduce wear and tear on your engine.

A proven power-lifter, the 27-year-old Doncic is this season handling the heaviest workload (39.8% usage rate) in the NBA and in his career, while logging 35.9 taxing minutes per game.

Lakers guard Luka Doncic reacts after sinking a three-point shot to give the Lakers a five-point lead against the Trail Blazers in the third quarter Friday night at Crypto.com Arena. (Gina Ferazzi / Los Angeles Times)

He's being challenged, pressed and trapped. He's accelerating and decelerating and accelerating again. He's charge-taking, pump-faking, piling up hoops-and-harms. Manipulating defenses and defending like he's taken some slander personally. Arguing with officials and heaving vibey buzzer-beaters from all over the building, including a 61-footer that completely altered the complexion of Friday's game, giving the Lakers momentum for the first time entering intermission.

And, no, he doesn't need to play heavy minutes to prepare to play heavy minutes in the playoffs. He also doesn't need to be wrapped in bubble wrap, but ideally he'd ramp up for the anchor leg instead of sprinting for the full marathon.

Remember what happened last season, after Doncic set the league on fire in March, averaging 37.5 points per game as the Lakers went 15-2 and announced themselves as challengers? He suffered a Grade 2 hamstring strain on April 2 that sidelined him for the rest of the season and doused the Lakers' hopes.

And look around now; the league is a cautionary tale of the tape. Anthony Edwards, Chet Holmgren, Ja Morant, Tyrese Haliburton, Jalen Williams are among the stars who've been lost to injuries.

The Lakers — who are starting the season by playing four weeks without a single two-day break between games — don't want to be included in the discussion about what's ailing the NBA's highest-usage talent this season.

It might be that the game has evolved to become more grueling, that teams are averaging more possessions per game, that possessions are shorter and that defenders are picking up ball-handlers sooner.

But it's not, Portland coach Micah Nori said, because guys aren't in shape: "They all have individual trainers, and they all work extremely hard, and they put in a lot of time — essentially 12 months out of the year. Back in the day, no disrespect to those guys, but that's why training camp was so long, because they needed training camp to get back in shape. And so now they're never out of shape, and I don't know if that has any bearing … but that's the only difference I see.

That includes Doncic. "He is the best shape I've ever seen him in," Nori said, proclaiming the Lakers' star his (way-too-early) favorite for MVP.

Shohei Ohtani being dead set on chasing the Cy Young Award killed the Dodgers' chances at a three-peat. And Doncic doing too much and earning his first MVP honor wouldn't do anything for the Lakers' championship chances if he's spent by the time the postseason starts.

#2774. "It's going to be amazing" – Campbell on Dortmund return

Signal Iduna Park was home for Cole Campbell for four years, but on Saturday, the American will be on the opposite side. The forward left Borussia Dortmund for newly-promoted Elversberg in the summer, where he has hit the ground running.

"I’ve had confidence in what I can do, and I am very grateful that Elversberg has put the trust in me and given me the confidence back," said Campbell in an interview with the DFL. "It’s been amazing to be here and to feel the trust and confidence that they have in me, so I am very happy to be here."

Campbell scored his first Bundesliga goal in Elversberg's opener, a surprise 3-2 win over Bayer Leverkusen. Since then, he's been moved to more of a bench role, partially due to injuries and partially to the emergence of other Elversberg attackers, like Maurice Krattenmacher.

Still, Campbell has made an impact when he's played. He scored with an acrobatic kick against Mainz to clinch a 4-1 win, taking Elversberg up to seventh in the Bundesliga. It was just his second top-flight goal.

“It was an amazing feeling for me to score a goal like this,” said Campbell. "I was very happy after the game and was also happy to have helped the team secure the win."

Campbell was only 18 when he made his debut in the Champions League, coming off the bench in front of a packed stadium against Sturm Graz. He replaced Jamie Gittens as Dortmund, then led by Nuri Şahin, snatched a dramatic 1-0 win at the death.

“At that point, it was probably one of my best feelings, and it was a dream come true to make my debut in the Champions League,” said Campbell. "To play in the Signal Iduna Park was also a different feeling, and I am really looking forward to getting to play there again this weekend. It was an amazing feeling for me.”

After four years and just seven appearances, Campbell left Dortmund in search of minutes. He joined Hoffenheim on loan last January, but injuries limited him to only five appearances. He was an unused substitute when Hoffenheim took on Dortmund in April.

That is unlikely to be the case this season. With the exception of the Augsburg match, which he missed because of an injury, Campbell has played every match this season for Elversberg. Even if he doesn't start, it's still likely he comes off the bench for a reunion with Niko Kovač's Borussia Dortmund and Signal Iduna Park.

“It’s a lot of emotions, and it will be very weird to be there and to not be in a Dortmund jersey,” said Campbell. "I am really looking forward to it, and I am very excited to see my friends and old teammates. I think it will be a special moment for me.”

Campbell debuted for the United States national team in October, coming off the bench in a 1-0 win over Canada.

The winger was also eligible for Iceland through his mother's side, initially playing there at youth level. While he's committed to the United States, Campbell takes the influence of both countries with him.

“It’s a mix of both,” said Campbell in an interview with the DFL. "I would say I take a little bit of both, but I feel more at home in the US for sure.”

Campbell was born in Houston, Texas, but his mother was part of the Iceland national team. He moved to Iceland at a young age, and when he was 15, Campbell was playing in Iceland's top flight. He stayed in the country for two years before leaving for Borussia Dortmund.

“I would say I feel more American, but I also like certain parts of Iceland, and a lot of my friends are from there,” said Campbell. “My mom, my grandma, and lots of my family are from there, so I love to go back there to visit."

#2773. Rams vs. Commanders: How to watch, start time, prediction and odds

The Rams' trip across the country to play the Washington Commanders on Sunday will be a homecoming of sorts for coach Sean McVay, safety Kam Curl and cornerback Emmanuel Forbes Jr.

McVay was a Washington assistant for seven years before the Rams hired him in 2017 and made the then-30-year-old McVay the youngest coach in modern NFL history. McVay was an assistant tight ends coach and tight ends coach under Mike Shanahan and offensive coordinator under Jay Gruden.

"I look back and think of what a pain in the butt I was as an OC, now being in this chair, and how patient [Gruden] was with me and how protected I really felt," said McVay, who guided the Rams to a road victory over the Commanders in 2020.

Curl played his first four NFL seasons for the Commanders after they selected him in the seventh round of the 2020 draft out of Arkansas. The Commanders did not re-sign him, and he joined the Rams on a two-year contract that included $6 million in guarantees.

Curl made several big plays for the Rams — including last season's game-clinching interception in the NFL divisional-round victory over the Chicago Bears — and the Rams gave him a three-year extension that includes $24 million in guarantees.

"Had a little bitter breakup, you know, but it is what it is at this point," Curl said of the Commanders. "I haven't been back to [the region] since, so it's going to feel good. Somewhat at home. Emotions will probably be high but keep them in check. ... It's going to be fun."

The Commanders selected Forbes with the 16 overall pick in the 2023 draft. He struggled as a rookie and was waived during the next season. The Rams claimed Forbes, and he has regained confidence mostly as a rotational player. With Jaylen Watson out for the season because of a shoulder injury, Josh Wallace and Forbes could see a lot of action.

Forbes said is "a way different player and a way different person" than he was during his time with the Commanders.

"Things happen and it's in the past,: he said, "but we'll be ready to go."

#2772. Cam Newton shares the only way Shedeur Sanders can become the Browns’ starting QB

Shedeur Sanders has been named as the starting quarterback for the Cleveland Browns this weekend as they face the New Orleans Saints.

Todd Monken confirmed on Friday that it would be Sanders taking the starting role for the Browns, with Deshaun Watson working his way through the concussion protocol following the recent loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers.

Sunday will mark the first start of the season for Sanders, who has been forced to watch from the sideline after Watson won the job over the offseason. However, the controversial young quarterback now has the opportunity to prove himself under Monken in a game situation.

Given the impressive season Watson has enjoyed so far for the Browns, former NFL quarterback Cam Newton has laid out exactly what it would take for Sanders to make the starting role his own.

So far this season, Sanders has only thrown three passes across two games in the NFL. The 24-year-old completed both of his passes last weekend when he came into the game against the Steelers, and he has shown his confidence ahead of the game against the Saints.

"The only way I see Shedeur Sanders starting for the rest of the season if they exceed any type of benchmark that was set like if I think it was like 300 yards plus," said Newton on his YouTube channel.

"If they have a 400-yard offensive day, oh man, we got to reconsider some stuff."

The chances of that happening against the Saints may not be as unlikely as Newton may think, though. The New Orleans Saints' defense has allowed 372 yards of total offense per game on average this season.

However, even with Watson at quarterback, the Saints have only managed to average 301 yards of total offense per game this season. So, sealing a 400-yard game with Sanders at quarterback would certainly be something.

#2770. LeBron James has become the king without a home

CLEVELAND — The opposite of love isn't hate, it's apathy.

LeBron James has gotten many receptions from Cleveland Cavaliers fans over his 24 seasons in the league. None have been as half-hearted and uncarring as Friday's.

There's always been a certain buzz in the arena when James plays in Cleveland. That has been the case since he was in high school.

That juice, however, was lacking in his first trip back home in a Philadelphia 76ers uniform. There were empty seats before tip-off. The ovation for him when he was announced in the starting lineups was positive, but hardly more than respectful. No tribute video was played, as has been the case for the last eight seasons. There were smatterings of boos and cheers throughout the night, but nothing more than what any other high-profile player gets at Rocket Arena. And a good number of fans were content heading out while James was still on the court.

In short, LeBron was just another guy participating in one of 41 home games against the Cavs.

"At this point it's become normal," Donovan Mitchell said of James's return. "My first year, you see it, and now it's just, we're playing the Sixers, to be honest. You obviously understand that the stands are going to be packed and obviously cheer for him, and rightfully so. He's a champion, he's from here, and he deserves all that and more for what he's done for the city. At this point it's just regular. … For us it's normal."

The normality of this reception stands in stark contrast to what we saw last year. Then, the crowd showered him with praise all game, ultimately moving him to tears. At the time, it seemed unfathomable that he would receive anything but love in the building he called home for 11 years. This summer, however, changed that.

James chose to leave the Los Angeles Lakers in free agency at the end of June. He then spent the first three weeks in July dragging his feet, leading those within the city and organization to believe he was returning to Cleveland. But then James threw a curveball and decided to go to a city he had no previous connection with and build a super team with the 76ers.

LeBron has earned the right to ring chase at the age of 41. But that comes with consequences, especially when you choose a conference rival over returning to a good team back home that also has a chance of winning a championship.

We saw the fallout of that choice on Friday night. There wasn't the pain and vitriol from 2010. There wasn't the love in all of his returns since 2018. Just emptiness.

LeBron understandably preferred this reaction to what he got when he first returned as a member of the Miami Heat. "Nothing can get as worse as December 2, 2010, from a reception standpoint," James said. "I've seen the end of the depths of hell when it comes to a reception here."

That night in 2010 was an absolute disaster. Cleveland should've handled that moment better. They have deserved all of the blame and condemnation that has come from how they handled that. Yet, hate comes from a place of passion. It comes from pain, an emotion that's real. Fans cared about what happened that night.

On Friday, I'm not sure if anyone cared too much anymore. There was appreciation, but there wasn't undying love. There was frustration, but not enough to actually voice that displeasure. Just a tiredness of a decades-long relationship that keeps oscillating back and forth, without either side really being sure how much they mean to the other.

That uncarrying is the saddest place a relationship can find itself, especially one as personal as this. Arguably no professional athlete has meant more to a region than LeBron to Northeast Ohio. The journey from being the teenage prodigy from Akron to delivering the first professional championship in over half a century for a sports-starved region is truly impossible to put into words.

The relationship between LeBron and northeast Ohio will continue in some form beyond this. Maybe that appreciation is there if he plays future games in Cleveland. And most likely, that outpouring of love will return for the inevitable statue and jersey retirement ceremonies.

But then again, that isn't guaranteed. James's choice to presumably end his career in a different uniform could just be the straw that broke the camel's back. The rift that caused both sides to continue drifting apart forever.

Friday could have been LeBron's last professional game in Northeast Ohio. Nothing about the future is guaranteed. And if so, there couldn't have been a more pitiful way for things to end in Cleveland.

#2768. Alexander Ovechkin announces this will be his last NHL season: 'Let's have fun'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2767. ‘Make sure you smile’: Rutgers coach Steve Pikiell continues to preach positivity amid cancer battle

Rutgers coach Steve Pikiell was on campus the day before his team's season opener against New Haven, and he sent a message to acting head coach Brandin Knight hours before tipoff.

"It's funny, he said, 'Make sure you smile,'" Knight recalled following the Scarlet Knights' 81-54 victory at Jersey Mike's Arena. "That was one of his big things, like have fun, enjoy it. It's always about the guys but have a good time and smile. That's the way he is. He can find some positivity in anything.

Pikiell, 58, announced that he was battling cancer in September, and Knight, the 44-year-old who was brought on Pikiell's staff in 2016 and had been his associate head coach the previous five seasons, was tabbed as acting head coach. While Pikiell focuses on his health, Knight draws inspiration from his boss, who contributes his time and thoughts where and when he can as he cycles through treatments and rests.

"Coach is one of the strongest people I know," Knight said. "He's showing up here two or three times. He is showing how tough he is. It's not easy to get out of bed and do things like that, but he comes around. He'll sit and watch practice. He'll give encouraging words."

Pikiell was not among the spectators at Jersey Mike's Arena, but support for his fight was evident throughout the crowd with students and fans wearing red T-shirts emblazoned with "Rutgers Tough" across the chest. They were selling for $30, with 100 percent of proceeds going to RWJ Barnabas Health's efforts in cancer treatment and patient care as part of a fundraiser envisioned by Pikiell.

A video of former players like Caleb McConnell, Dylan Harper, Ace Bailey and Ron Harper Jr. talking about different examples of being "Rutgers Tough"played on the scoreboard above center court. Knight noted that the shirts sold out in the first day. Players will continue to wear them during warmups this season. The first $250,000 of the campaign is coming from Pikiell and his wife, Kate,

"I hope it's inspiring not only to myself and all of these guys," Knight said. "Whatever you're going through, whatever type of adversity you think you're dealing with right now, it is nothing like the kind coach and his family has been dealing with."

Knight carried on the program's signature approach to defense against New Haven, which is in its second season in Division I and the second year of a three-year transition from Division II. The Scarlet Knights forced 17 turnovers with a mix of different looks, including full court pressure. In all, the team collected 10 steals, three of which were credited to Davis, a senior reserve who finished with 13 points on 5 of 5 shooting.

"We just wanted to be as active as possible," Davis said. "You know, B Knight just wanted us to speed them up, bring the fight to them. The full court got our energy up, kind of got us going."

Fifteen players logged at least two minutes as Knight worked to find the best rotation of talent that has been assembled by retaining guards like Tariq Francis and Jamichael Davis and bringing in transfers like Rasheed Jones and Christian Gurdak.

Does Joe Buck deserve $17 million a year, and should Troy Aikman even care, or know how much his partner is making? The guy's a Hall of Fame quarterback, and as such, should be able to deal with life's unfairness, if whatever he makes can be considered unfair.

Again, this is an insult to the workers, all of them, who barely can make ends meet. Both these guys should be grateful that life is unfair, but not if you're making millions of dollars for flapping your lips about a game.

When I open my L.A. Times in the morning, I go directly to the sports section and search for Bill Plaschke's column. I love his style and especially his wit. So he has a prediction miss or two here and there, but no one puts a smile on my face more than him. Keep it up Bill, we all need more laughter in our lives.

#2764. 2. Bundesliga preview: Dynamo Dresden vs. Greuther Fürth

Dynamo Dresden will be looking to end their recent league struggles when they welcome Greuther Fürth on Friday evening, with Thomas Stamm’s side desperate for points as they look to climb away from the bottom of the 2. Bundesliga table.

The hosts head into the Matchday 11 encounter following a disappointing 2-1 defeat against Hannover 96 last weekend. Despite taking the lead through Nicolai Rapp, Dresden were unable to hold onto their advantage, with a second-half comeback leaving them bottom of the table on eight points.

Greuther Fürth, meanwhile, arrive in Saxony with renewed confidence after securing a narrow 1-0 victory over Holstein Kiel. Aaron Keller’s 87th-minute winner secured their third league victory of the campaign, moving Heiko Vogel’s side into ninth place with 12 points.

With just four points separating the two sides, Friday’s encounter presents an important opportunity for both teams to build some momentum heading into the next international break.

Dynamo Dresden have endured an inconsistent return to the second tier since promotion a few years ago and this season is no different, with two victories, two draws and six defeats from their opening ten league fixtures leaving them rooted to the foot of the table.

Stamm’s side have struggled particularly with defensive consistency, conceding 20 goals so far this season while finding the net on 12 occasions.

However, there have been encouraging signs in front of their home supporters. Dresden secured an impressive 2-0 derby victory over 1. FC Magdeburg before following that result with another 2-0 win against Schalke 04 in the DFB-Pokal.

Those performances will offer encouragement ahead of Friday’s encounter, particularly given Fürth’s own struggles for consistency this season.

The defeat against Hannover was nevertheless another frustrating setback. Dresden had looked capable of taking something from the encounter before Friedrich Müller’s dismissal allowed the hosts to take control, with the defender now unavailable for the visit of Fürth.

Stamm will therefore be demanding a response from his players, particularly in their defensive organisation and ability to maintain their intensity throughout the full 90 minutes.

Speaking ahead of the game, the Dynamo head coach acknowledged the quality of the opposition but insisted his side should approach the encounter with confidence.

“I expect a team that plays bravely with the ball and intensely against it. They resolve difficult situations with purpose. We need a really good performance, but we don’t need to hide at home.”

Stamm also stressed the importance of remaining positive, urging his players not to become frustrated if their early opportunities fail to find the back of the net.

Greuther Fürth travel to Dresden looking to build on their recent victory over Holstein Kiel, which ended a frustrating run of results and provided a welcome boost for Vogel’s side.

The visitors have collected 12 points from their opening ten league fixtures, recording three victories, three draws and four defeats. Their 13 goals scored suggest they possess some attacking quality, although 16 goals conceded highlight an area that still requires improvement.

Fürth’s biggest challenge this season has arguably been finding consistency. Their victory over Eintracht Braunschweig was followed by a disappointing 3-0 defeat against Osnabrück, before they returned to winning ways against Kiel.

The late nature of their most recent victory should nevertheless provide some confidence, with Aaron Keller finding the net in the 87th minute to secure all three points.

Vogel will be hoping his side can now register consecutive league victories for the first time this season, although he is well aware of the difficulties associated with travelling to Dresden.

The Fürth head coach has called for a better balance between defensive organisation and attacking intent, particularly after his side struggled to create opportunities in recent outings.

“Good positioning in attack is always the foundation for creating scoring opportunities. We need to be more precise in that area than we have been in recent matches.” Vogel explained ahead of the encounter.

The visitors will also be keen to avoid a repeat of their previous trip to Dresden, when they suffered a 2-0 defeat in January.

With experienced attacking players such as the league’s joint top-scorer Felix Klaus alongside the creativity of Ole Pohlmann, Fürth will certainly possess the tools to trouble their hosts if they can find the right balance going forward.

Friday’s encounter will be the 19th competitive meeting between the two sides, with Greuther Fürth holding the historical advantage.

The visitors have recorded nine victories compared to Dynamo Dresden’s four, while the remaining five encounters have ended in draws.

However, Dresden will take encouragement from their most recent meeting, which took place at the Rudolf-Harbig-Stadion in January 2026.

Goals from Thomas Keller and Jakob Lemmer secured a convincing 2-0 victory for the hosts, marking the beginning of an important run of results in their battle to secure survival last season.

Interestingly, that victory was Fürth’s only defeat in their previous nine meetings with Dresden, with the Franken side recording five victories and three draws during that period.

Vogel’s men will therefore be hoping to reassert their historical dominance, while Dresden will be looking to repeat their January performance and secure another important home victory.

Dynamo Dresden have several important absentees to contend with ahead of Friday’s fixture, particularly in the defensive department.

Friedrich Müller is suspended following his red card against Hannover, while Brooklyn Ezeh is also unavailable due to suspension following his dismissal for the club’s Under-21 side.

Lars Bünning and Kenneth Schmidt remain sidelined with longer-term injuries, while Thomas Keller continues to be unavailable following his concussion.

Luca Herrmann has also joined the injury list after picking up an injury against Hannover.

For Greuther Fürth, Maxim Dal remains sidelined through injury, although Vogel should otherwise have a relatively settled squad available.

#2762. Five takeaways from Norwich City's latest accounts

Norwich City Football Club has released its latest annual report, detailing the club's financial standing for the year until 30 June 2026.

It shows the Canaries recorded an operating loss of £13.3m - despite making almost £46m in profit from selling players.

Before taking player trading into account, the club recorded an operating loss of £42.3m, compared with a £25.5m loss in 2025.​

While the Championship side reported increases in areas including attendances, retail and sponsorship, its operating costs also rose sharply.

Here are five key takeaways from the club's latest annual report.

Staff costs have increased at Norwich City [Press Association]

According to the report, the club's operating costs rose to £99.8m, from £79.2m the previous year.

Norwich City said this reflected its "continued investment in the playing squad and football operations".

A large chunk of this figure is staff costs, which rose from £48.1m the previous year to £57.9m in 2026.

These costs included wages, National Insurance, pensions and other employment costs.

Within that figure, wages and salaries rose from £39.9m to £49.6m.

Norwich City striker Josh Sargent completed a move to Toronto FC in a deal worth more than £20m [Press Association]

Norwich City did record significant profit from player sales.

The departure of players such as Borja Sainz, Jonathan Rowe and Josh Sargent helped earn the club £45.9m profit from player trading, up from the £24.3m achieved in the previous year.

The accounts also included £16.8m in player amortisation, an accounting process that spreads the transfer fees paid for players over the lengths of their contracts.

After player trading was taken into account, the club's operating loss fell from £42.3m to £13.3m, which it said was "broadly consistent with the prior year's result".

In the report the club said: "Player trading remains an important part of our financial model and generated profits of £45.9 million during the year, helping to offset underlying operating losses."

Fan support has remained strong with a slight increase in shirt sales [Press Association]

The average attendance at Norwich City's Carrow Road stadium was 25,899, while the club sold 20,039 season tickets.

The club described this as "another strong year" for ticket sales.

Retail revenue increased to £2.4m, helped by an 8.6% increase in replica shirt sales, with more than 29,000 shirts sold during the season.

The report said figures showed "the incredible loyalty and commitment of our fanbase."

During this period the club has signed new players such as Mathias Kvistgaarden [Press Association]

Norwich City has invested heavily in signing new players, with the accounting value of its player registrations rising from £32.6m to £53.9m.

The accounts show £42.9m was added to player registrations during the year.

This figure could include agent's fees, transfer fees and other costs linked to those deals.

Those new signings include Mathias Kvistgaarden, Jovon Makama and Pelle Mattsson.

The club said the figure "reflects the club's commitment to strengthening its squad while maintaining a strategy focused on recruitment and player development".

There has been increased support for Norwich City Women [Getty Images]

Support for Norwich City Women increased during the season with the team winning promotion to the third tier.

There was an increase in attendance and sponsorship for the side, with a 20% increase in Women's season ticket sales.

Attendance at matches played at The Nest increased by 26%.

According to the report, the growth of the women's team has been reflected in an increased sponsorship income.

It said: "Sponsorship revenues also increased, supported by a more integrated approach to commercial rights across both the men's and women's teams."

During the financial year the income from commercial partnership across the club increased by more than £200,000 to £4.6m.

#2759. NBA's biggest winners and losers of the week: Last unbeaten team is ... the Grizzlies? Plus a crisis in OKC

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

We couldn't even settle in before the season went sideways, could we? After a relatively ordinary first few days, the entire NBA seemed to catch the injury bug in Week 2. A seemingly endless list of All-Stars went down in the past seven days with injuries that will keep them out for periods ranging from a few weeks to, potentially, the entire season, and after just 13 days of basketball, the league-wide landscape suddenly looks completely different.

So let's look back on the week that was and rank some winners and losers from the NBA's last seven days.

Raise a glass for the NBA's last unbeaten team, the... Memphis Grizzlies? Huh? Yes, the Memphis Grizzlies, one of last season's most egregious tankers, are running roughshod over the rest of the NBA. As of Sunday afternoon, they rank...

Even after cooling off following his preposterously hot start, Ty Jerome has still made more runners (19) than all but a handful of players have attempted. Jerome may be cooling off, but Cam Boozer is heating up: the No. 3 overall pick just shot 50-44-100 for the week and picked up his first career triple-double in a win over the then-unbeaten Portland Trail Blazers (and former Grizzlies star Ja Morant). Nobody can miss a 3. Zech Edey and Isaiah Stewart are almost completely walling off the rim. Grizzlies opponents are taking only 19 shots per game in the restricted area.

The pick-and-roll-heavy scheme Tuomas Iisalo was known for abroad is finally coming together in the NBA. Only the Cleveland Cavaliers have generated more shots out of pick-and-roll than Memphis. Only the Miami Heat and Houston Rockets are scoring more points per possession on those shots. After Iisalo's short-stint rotations caused so much of an uproar last season, Memphis has gotten off to this start with nobody averaging even 32 minutes a game.

Memphis won't be this good forever. They've played a Charmin soft schedule. Eventually, they'll start missing 3s, and Jerome will probably settle somewhere between the MVP frontrunner he was in Week 1 and the far less effective player we saw in Week 2. But all of this winning isn't a fluke. It's not as though their opponents are just missing shots. They're killing the teams that they're playing. Even if 82-0 is unrealistic, a playoff berth certainly feels realistic for a Grizzlies team that is thriving to start the season.

Nobody roots for injuries, but teams certainly benefit from them. We came into the season assuming the Thunder and Spurs were heavy championship favorites. The Thunder are suddenly in peril, and the Rockets beat San Antonio head-to-head in the season's opening week. They have one of the few big men in the NBA in Alperen Sengun who seems genuinely comfortable attacking Victor Wembanyama. He shot 17 of 23 against Wembanyama as the primary defender last season, according to NBA.com tracking data. He just dropped a 29-7-7 on him in Houston's second game of the year. The stars are aligning for the Rockets already.

This isn't purely a matter of circumstance, either. Houston has clearly leveled up with Fred VanVleet back in the fold. They'd likely be standing alongside the Grizzlies in the ranks of the undefeated had Sengun not missed Friday's loss to the Dallas Mavericks. After a year of consternation about their mess of a half-court offense, Houston ranks fourth in the NBA in points per 100 half-court plays thus far this season. They have the NBA's No. 1 overall offense despite barely getting any minutes out Steven Adams so far. Just imagine how easily they'll score with his offensive rebounding in the mix.

The season is far too young to say anything definitively, especially with injuries coming so quickly. For now, at least, Houston should feel relatively safe about outwinning Oklahoma City in the regular season, and it has a one-game lead and a head-to-head victory over San Antonio in its back pocket. The No. 1 seed feels much more attainable to them than it did two weeks ago, and with it would come the easiest possible path to the NBA Finals.

The consensus surrounding Lendeborg as a draft prospect was that, as a 24-year-old on opening night, he would arrive in the NBA as a productive player, but would have limited upside to grow beyond that. He's older than Jonathan Kuminga, after all, so it's not as though his arrival heralded the emergence of yet another timeline. At this rate, though, it might not matter if Lendeborg has already peaked as an NBA player, because the last week suggests he might have arrived in the NBA as a star.

His collegiate career-high in scoring was 30 points. He's topped that figure twice in the last week alone, and it's not as though he's doing that with crazy volume. His season-high in shot attempts (20) is Darius Acuff's season-low. His only bad game of the week came in his hyped rematch with Luka Dončić... a game the Golden State Warriors still managed to win despite Lendeborg claiming he "wet the bed."

Lendeborg's emergence has a chance to be genuinely transformative for Golden State. Suddenly the Warriors have the secondary scorer they need next to Curry. When Jimmy Butler returns, they'll have one of the most physically imposing pairs of forwards in the NBA, helping to offset their size issues at center with Kristaps Porziņģis sidelined. Maybe Lendeborg is even good enough to compel Golden State to attach draft picks to Porziņģis' contract and go make a win-now move. A week ago, the Warriors were winless and limping their way through a hopeless season. They've since won four straight and generated their first real dose of optimism since Butler tore his ACL, and it's almost entirely because of a rookie that somehow slipped out of the top 10 of the draft.

On Monday, the Thunder announced that both Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace would have surgeries that could end their seasons. That night, they lost Alex Caruso to a sprained ankle. That's a year's worth of injury news in a night, and then on Friday, it came out Chet Holmgren has a small patellar tendon tear that will require an 8-10 week absence following a "biological" treatment. What exactly that means for his long-term health prospects is unclear.

The Thunder opened the season by avenging their Western Conference Finals loss to the San Antonio Spurs. They followed that up by dispatching the player team that pushed them to the brink in the 2025 playoffs: Nikola Jokić and the Denver Nuggets. They looked like heavy championship favorites.

Now? It's possible that they reached the point of no return on injuries before Halloween, and if they haven't now, they could at any moment. We went from "the Thunder are the best team in the NBA" to "the Thunder could trade their way back into the championship picture" to "does it really make sense for the Thunder to start their luxury tax in this nightmare season?" all in the span of a few days. That last question is still months away from an answer, but the fact that it's even on the table is a testament to just how disastrous the last week or so has been in Oklahoma City.

We have our first reports of an unhappy team in this early season, and it is one of last year's surprise success stories: the Phoenix Suns. On Thursday, Chris Haynes explained that "there is some growing frustration within that locker room for the simple fact that that roster does not have a point guard that can organize that offense."

We should clarify here that the Suns do have a point guard on their roster... they're just not starting him. The Suns are scoring 123.2 points per 100 possessions with Collin Gillespie on the floor... and 106.4 with him off it, according to Cleaning the Glass. Pretty much all of the underlying numbers suggest that simply starting Gillespie over Jalen Green could solve some of these point guard issues. The Suns assist on 76.3% of their baskets with Gillespie on the floor so far this season, but only 54.2% of them with him off it. Devin Booker has a 68.1% true shooting percentage with Gillespie playing and a 51.3% mark without him.

The decision to start Green was a questionable one even before the season started. He wasn't really a part of last season's success. He was a No. 2 overall pick, sure, but that was for a different team. The Suns don't have enough invested in Green to justify the continued usage of these suboptimal lineups. They frankly have too many real problems to continue creating more of them for themselves with suboptimal lineup decisions.

The Suns had a top-10 defense a year ago. They rank 30th early in this season. Their dominant offensive rebounding has slipped to the middle of the pack as well, and even their turnover rate has ticked up a bit. The Suns beat expectations last season because they were disciplined and they played harder than anyone in the league. They've fallen from No. 5 to No. 26 in deflections per game this season, and No. 6 to No. 26 in loose ball recoveries. These aren't the hustle Suns of a year ago, at least thus far. Some of that can be traced back to the players taking on new prominence this season. Green isn't exactly known as a high-energy player. Neither is Miles Bridges, who has thus far underwhelmed following Phoenix's decision to trade an unprotected first-round pick for him over the summer.

The Suns were the feel-good story of last season. Going from that to the first team to leak displeasure to the press this season is a pretty precipitous drop. A point guard upgrade, internal or external, isn't going to address everything wrong with this team.

The Jazz are actually trying to win for the first time in the Will Hardy era... yet they're playing worse than they did when they were trying to lose. Utah's 1-5 start is the second-worst of Hardy's tenure in Utah, trailing only the six-game losing streak that kicked off their 2024-25 season. Utah's offense -- vaunted for thriving with limited resources at points during the Jazz rebuild -- is scoring fewer points per 100 possessions (105.3) than it did in any full season during the Hardy era.

The loss of the perpetually injury-prone Jaren Jackson Jr. to a torn MCL this week brought several major decisions Utah has made over the past year or so into question. The Jazz gave up three first-round picks to get Jackson on a max deal, and he's thus far given them nine games. They traded Walker Kessler and passed on Cam Boozer in the NBA Draft in part because they had Jackson. Kessler's Lakers are 5-2, and Boozer is competing with Lendeborg to become the early Rookie of the Year frontrunner. No. 2 overall pick Darryn Peterson has been by far the least impressive of the top four picks in June's draft thus far and was even benched down the stretch of an overtime loss to the San Antonio Spurs.

We're six games into the season. It is much too early to panic over the state of the Jazz. But after punting four full seasons to get where they are now, Utah certainly expected more than it has gotten thus far, and with Jackson injured, there's no telling when or if the Jazz will be able to turn things around.

Tampa Bay attempts to complete a sweep of the 2026 ALDS when they square off against New York at 8 p.m. ET in Game 3 on Wednesday at Yankee Stadium. The Rays, who defeated the Yankees in this round in 2020 en route to the second World Series appearance in franchise history, edged New York 1-0 in this year's series opener before pushing their AL East rivals to the brink of elimination with a 5-2 victory in Game 2.

The Rays went 7-6 against New York during the regular season but lost four of the six contests at Yankee Stadium, including three of four in their penultimate series of the campaign. Tampa Bay was outscored 15-6 in its final two games in the Bronx, but its pitching staff has kept the Yankees in check thus far in the ALDS.

New York was limited to one hit in Game 1 as Drew Rasmussen had a no-hitter for 7 2/3 innings before Austin Wells ripped a double down the right field line. However, Wells made an ill-advised decision to try and stretch it into a triple and was thrown out easily at third base. Rays closer Bryan Baker worked a perfect ninth to preserve the win.

The Yankees didn't fare much better offensively in Game 2 as they registered just four hits, two of which were solo homers by Ben Rice. They were even worse defensively, committing four errors -- including three in the first inning that helped give Tampa Bay a 1-0 lead.

Tampa Bay will look to punch its ticket to the ALCS behind Nick Martinez, who set a career high with 15 wins this year and matched another with a 3.10 ERA.
